Where it began

Graeme Swann was born in Northampton on 24 March 1979 and went to Sponne School in Towcester. He started out with his home county, Northamptonshire, making his debut in 1997, and the following year he was part of the England side that won the Under-19 World Cup in South Africa.

The road to the top was not quick. He played a single one-day international in 2000, which did not go to plan, and then waited seven years for another chance. In the meantime he moved to Nottinghamshire in 2005, and a strong 2007 season brought him back into the England side.

The player

When the Test call finally came, he wasted no time. On debut against India in December 2008 he had Gautam Gambhir lbw with his third ball and Rahul Dravid lbw with his sixth, only the second man in Test history to take two wickets in his first over. He played 60 Tests between 2008 and 2013 and took 255 wickets at 29.97, with 17 five-wicket hauls, three ten-wicket matches and a best of 6 for 65.

The high points came thick and fast. He took the last Australian wicket at The Oval in 2009 to win back the Ashes. No English spinner before him had taken 50 wickets in a calendar year, as he did in 2009. In 2010 he took ten in a match in Bangladesh, something no English off-spinner had done since Jim Laker. He helped win the World Twenty20 in 2010, the Ashes in Australia that winter, and the No. 1 Test ranking in 2011, when he also spent time as the top-ranked one-day bowler in the world.

What made him special

He bowled to take wickets, not to save runs. He gave the ball plenty of air and bounce, varied his pace cleverly, and used an arm ball and a slider he called his flying saucer ball rather than a mystery delivery. He often stood at second slip, too, and held 54 Test catches.

With the bat he was a busy, quick-scoring lower-order man who made 1,370 Test runs. The Test hundred never quite came, though. His best was 85 against South Africa in 2009.

Away from the middle

He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and ECB Cricketer of the Year in 2010. After retiring from cricket in December 2013 he joined Test Match Special as a summariser in 2014, and he was part of TNT's commentary team for the 2025–26 Ashes in Australia.

In 2018 he swapped pads for dancing shoes on Strictly Come Dancing, partnered by Oti Mabuse, and the pair reached week 10. He was also the lead singer of a covers band called Dr Comfort and the Lurid Revelations, playing gigs around Nottinghamshire.

And finally

For a man who once had to wait seven years between international games, he made up for lost time remarkably quickly. He had been made to wait, and he spent the next five years making batters wait too, for a ball they could safely hit.
